source: J. J. Fux, Gradus ad Parnassum (1725), trans. A. Mann, The Study of Counterpoint (Norton 1965)

intro.title: The Study of Counterpoint a guide to the five species, with scores you can hear and exercises that check themselves

paragraphs.html: Fux teaches counterpoint as a staircase. You climb from note against note to florid writing in two voices, then climb again in three and in four. This guide follows his table of contents. Each chapter lists the rules Fux treats as binding, the guidelines he gives as advice, and the figures and exercises of the book. Every score plays on a synthesized harpsichord. Every exercise workbench checks your notes against the rules as you write.

prose.html: Mann compares the study of counterpoint with the study of perspective. Both grew from the Renaissance turn toward three-dimensional thought. Medieval discantus stacked parts like the levels of a landscape. Contrapunctus, from punctus contra punctum (point against point, note against note), appears around 1300. By 1412 Prosdocimus speaks of cantus contra cantum: judging a whole melody against another.
prose.text: Mann compares the study of counterpoint with the study of perspective. Both grew from the Renaissance turn toward three-dimensional thought. Medieval discantus stacked parts like the levels of a landscape. Contrapunctus, from punctus contra punctum (point against point, note against note), appears around 1300. By 1412 Prosdocimus speaks of cantus contra cantum: judging a whole melody against another.

prose.html: Tinctoris separates simple counterpoint (equal notes) from diminished or florid counterpoint (several notes against one), and prefers the second: “the variety of proportions produces the most agreeable counterpoint.” Zarlino sums up the Renaissance. Monteverdi’s “second practice” splits the old style from the new. Fux, publishing in 1725, deliberately chooses Palestrina’s style (the stile antico) as the basis for teaching and places three intermediate species between simple and florid counterpoint.

prose.html: The book’s influence runs through Haydn (who worked every exercise), Leopold and Wolfgang Mozart (Attwood’s studies), Beethoven (via Albrechtsberger, Fux’s successor at St. Stephen’s), Brahms, Strauss and Hindemith.

chapters.title: The Author’s Foreword

prose.html: Fux writes for young people “who lack means and a teacher.” His method copies the way children learn letters, then syllables, then words. He gives little space to theory and much to practice, “since action is the test of excellence.”

prose.html: The book is a dialogue. Aloysius, the master, stands for Palestrina. Josephus is the pupil. Josephus writes; Aloysius corrects. Many rules appear only when a mistake prompts them, so the figures with “mistakes” are part of the teaching.

lede.html: Before the first exercise, Josephus must know which intervals are consonant, the three kinds of motion, and four rules that govern how consonances follow each other.

bookFigures.html: Direct motion: both parts move in the same direction, by step or skip.
bookFigures.text: Direct motion: both parts move in the same direction, by step or skip.

bookFigures.html: Contrary motion: one part rises while the other falls.

bookFigures.html: Oblique motion: one part moves while the other stays.

lede.html: The simplest species: two voices in notes of equal length (whole notes), consonances only. The given melody, the cantus firmus, never changes; you write a counterpoint above or below it.
lede.text: The simplest species: two voices in notes of equal length (whole notes), consonances only. The given melody, the cantus firmus, never changes; you write a counterpoint above or below it.

items.html: Equal note values; only consonances.
items.text: Equal note values; only consonances.

items.html: Begin and end with a perfect consonance. The beginning expresses perfection, the end relaxation.
items.text: Begin and end with a perfect consonance. The beginning expresses perfection, the end relaxation.

items.html: The counterpoint must be in the same mode as the cantus. Below the cantus, begin on the unison or octave, not the fifth.
items.text: The counterpoint must be in the same mode as the cantus. Below the cantus, begin on the unison or octave, not the fifth.

items.html: Next-to-last bar: a major sixth if the cantus is in the lower part, a minor third if it is in the upper part. The 7th degree is raised in D, G and A.
items.text: Next-to-last bar: a major sixth if the cantus is in the lower part, a minor third if it is in the upper part. The 7th degree is raised in D, G and A.

items.html: Obey the four rules: no parallel fifths or octaves, and no direct motion into a perfect consonance (hidden fifths and octaves become audible when the skip is filled in).
items.text: Obey the four rules: no parallel fifths or octaves, and no direct motion into a perfect consonance (hidden fifths and octaves become audible when the skip is filled in).

items.html: No augmented, diminished or chromatic melodic intervals; no skip larger than a fifth except the octave and the ascending minor sixth. The major sixth and the seventh are forbidden.
items.text: No augmented, diminished or chromatic melodic intervals; no skip larger than a fifth except the octave and the ascending minor sixth. The major sixth and the seventh are forbidden.

items.html: Mi contra fa: no tritone skip (F–B).
items.text: Mi contra fa: no tritone skip (F–B).

items.html: The unison only at the beginning and the end.
items.text: The unison only at the beginning and the end.

items.html: Never approach an octave or unison by skips in contrary motion from a remote consonance, even in more than two parts.
items.text: Never approach an octave or unison by skips in contrary motion from a remote consonance, even in more than two parts.

items.html: Modes may end only on D, E, F, G, A, C. B has no perfect fifth.
items.text: Modes may end only on D, E, F, G, A, C. B has no perfect fifth.

items.html: Use contrary and oblique motion as often as possible; they make mistakes easier to avoid.
items.text: Use contrary and oblique motion as often as possible; they make mistakes easier to avoid.

items.html: Use more imperfect than perfect consonances; imperfect ones are more harmonious.
items.text: Use more imperfect than perfect consonances; imperfect ones are more harmonious.

items.html: Repeat a tone only occasionally, and never more than once.
items.text: Repeat a tone only occasionally, and never more than once.

items.html: Not more than three or four parallel thirds or sixths in a row.
items.text: Not more than three or four parallel thirds or sixths in a row.

items.html: Avoid skips that follow each other in the same direction, and compensate a skip by turning back. Stay within a comfortable register.
items.text: Avoid skips that follow each other in the same direction, and compensate a skip by turning back. Stay within a comfortable register.

items.html: Even stepwise, avoid outlining a tritone unless the line continues in the same direction.
items.text: Even stepwise, avoid outlining a tritone unless the line continues in the same direction.

items.html: The ottava battuta (a tenth to an octave by contrary steps on the downbeat) is left to your discretion.
items.text: The ottava battuta (a tenth to an octave by contrary steps on the downbeat) is left to your discretion.

items.html: Leaving a unison by skip is bad in itself.
items.text: Leaving a unison by skip is bad in itself.

items.html: Fa leads down, mi leads up: a sharp can underline an ascent and avoid a harsh F/F♯ relation.

items.html: Voice crossing is a permitted expedient. Keep the voices close (neighbouring clefs).

lede.html: Two half notes on the same pitch, tied over the bar line: the first on the upbeat, the second on the downbeat. This is the ligature, or syncopation.

items.html: The upbeat half is always consonant. A consonant ligature has both halves consonant; a dissonant ligature has a dissonant downbeat.

items.html: A tied dissonance is the retardation of the following note. It must resolve down by step to the consonance that would stand on the downbeat if the retardation were removed.

fig5.title: Josephus’s first counterpoint, above the cantus in D
fig5.caption: Fifth at the start; 5→3 by oblique motion (the only use of repetition); 3→3 parallel; 3→5 contrary; 6–8 at the cadence with the raised C♯. Numbers between the staves are the intervals: blue = perfect, grey = imperfect.

fig6.title: Counterpoint below: two mistakes, then the correction
fig6.caption: As in Fux’s Fig. 6, the first attempt opens a fifth below (outside the mode) and moves from a third to a fifth in direct motion. The correction starts on the octave and stays on the low D, so a tenth moves to the fifth by contrary motion.

fig7.title: Hidden fifths revealed by diminution
fig7.caption: Bars 1–2: a third moves to a fifth by direct motion (Fig. 7). Bars 3–4: an octave moves to a fifth by direct motion (Fig. 8). Fill in the skip the way a singer would ornament it, and two real fifths appear (B♭–F → A–E; G–D → A–E). “The lawgivers of an art have set down nothing pointlessly.”

fig16.title: Octaves and unisons approached by contrary motion
fig16.caption: Bars 1–2: ottava battuta, a tenth to an octave by contrary steps. Fux “has long searched for the reason” it is forbidden and leaves it to your discretion. Bars 3–4: a unison reached from a third; the unison is avoided except at the start and end. Bars 5–6 and 7–8: an octave and a unison reached by skips from a remote consonance, “not to be tolerated even in composition for more than two voices.”

fig33.title: Second species above the cantus, corrected
fig33.caption: Upbeat dissonances (red figures) are all passing notes filling a third: A–B–C in bar 2, B–C–D in bar 5 and so on. The cadence is 5–6–8.

fig35.title: Second species below, beginning with a half rest
fig35.caption: Below the cantus the cadence becomes 5–3–1 (with C♯ as the minor third below E). Note the octave skip in bar 9 that makes room.

skip3.title: Does a skip hide fifths between downbeats?
skip3.caption: D–G and E–A are fifths on two downbeats. With a skip of a third (D–B) the ear still links them, so they count as consecutive fifths. With a skip of a fourth (D–G) the distance makes the ear “forget” the first downbeat (Figs. 30–32).

fig55.title: Third species above the cantus in D
fig55.caption: Bar 1 shows the stepwise pattern of Fig. 47: 1 consonant, 2 dissonant, 3 consonant, 4 dissonant. Bar 3 (8–7–5–6) is a cambiata: the dissonant seventh skips down a third to the fifth. B♭ appears where B would make mi contra fa against F.

cambiata.title: The nota cambiata
cambiata.caption: 8–7–5–6: the second quarter (D, a seventh) is dissonant and skips a third down to a consonance, then the line turns up by step. Strictly the skip belongs between the 1st and 2nd notes (Fig. 51), but filling it would need eighth notes, so the masters approved this form.

fig73.title: Fourth species above the cantus in D
fig73.caption: Upbeats consonant; downbeat sevenths (red) resolve down to sixths. Bar 5 drops the ligature: Josephus avoided repeating the ligature of bars 3–4. The cadence is 7–6–8.

eighths.title: Where eighth notes may go
eighths.caption: Bar 1: a pair of eighths on the 2nd quarter, moving by step, is good. Bar 2: eighths on the 1st quarter are bad. They are allowed on the 2nd and 4th quarters, never on the 1st and 3rd.

fig101.title: Three parts, note against note: cantus on top
fig101.caption: The harmonic triad stands in almost every bar (figures under the bass). Bars 7–8: the outer voices move into a fifth by direct motion, which Fux allows “if there is no other possibility, in order to avoid a worse awkwardness.” The final chord has no third.

fig160.title: Four parts: the model, cantus in the alto
fig160.caption: Each chord holds third, fifth and octave where possible. Fux numbers all intervals as simple numbers “so that the doubling of the consonances might be plainer to the eye.” Bar 4 has a fourth between inner voices, which is acceptable because intervals are reckoned from the bass.
